column1: A dark night spread its wings, behold a terrible hell has boiled, the whole earth trembles, a roar of a violent war is rising! Ah, what a cannonade! Ah, what an underground roar! The sky seems to fall before the terrible wrath of God. Black, Black, what are you? You are a toy in front of this! Here a terrible thunder is blowing, here a hellish roar is heard! Five meters away a hundred cannons sow here fire and death, still fresh, still new how they roar at you endlessly! Dante, Dante, why are you trembling, yellow as a lemon? How can you be so excited about this, Uncle Napoleon? Oh, Verdion, you have probably never heard such a powerful roar! Here a midnight battle is being fought with a cannonade of beans.

Who among the waters of the sea has had such great luck as Count Arnaldos had on the morning of San Juan! He was going hunting then, carrying a gray falcon in his hand, and he saw a galley heading towards the shore. The sails were of silk, the ropes were twisted from flax. And the sailor sang a strange little song in joy: from it the sea calmed down, the fury of the evil wind and the fish from the depths rose in flocks, on the mast countless birds perched in deep delight.'My galley, you, galley, may God protect you from evil and from the troubles of the sea, the wrath of the old ocean, from the plains of Almeria, from the isthmus of Gibraltar, from the Venetian Gulf, from the lowlands of Flanders and from the shores of Leon, a whirlwind of calamity and evil.' And Count Arnaldos spoke, listen to what he said: 'For God's sake, tell me this wonderful song, my sailor!' And the sailor answered him, his voice was frank: 'I will tell this song only to the one who goes with me.'

Earth, in whose bosom there is hatred and murder,Generation after generation,Bloody earth with all your burden of sin growing weight! How can you so easily follow your heavenly path, Around the sun that sees your wounds, And sees a light green wave Spring after spring? Yes, for the same One who has bound the earth The bond of laws, Who gave His people in the thunder of the desert mountain The law in their hands, — He lets His sun gild every poor straw,He is the God who hears the prayer of the dust,Who in the fullness of time gave us His Son. Therefore, if all our happiness should fade, Suddenly stand before fall, Always from earth an eternal hymn of thanks Shall rise; Therefore, however mighty the spirits of darkness work, Never shall our prayer sink to a sigh, Never shall the Church of the Lord be shaken a whit. Teach us then, Earth, on the eagle's wing of the Spirit, faithful as you, to swing about our high heavenly light in comforting remembrance,to draw from Him all the light that we desire,to draw from Him the warmth of life in our breast,to grow green for God's glory,to become golden for harvest.

And it was at Skanderborg Station that my thoughts flew away. I saw a pretty young person with hazel eyes. Coquettish eyes, but silent and pale, with features so sharp, a nineteen-year-old's bosom to a fine figure, slender and heavy hips. A chaste and daring bourgeois child with restless butterfly limbs, Of the arousing power of her gait and bearing I still sense a re-impression. For it is a memory from carefree years, before hypocrisy and vanity had crushed our young desire to death, if not our mouths had locked, When little was embraced, but much enjoyed, and everything and everyone desired, When the mind lay open and the blood free like the summer sea and the weather. I remember those brown eyes, how sad she became when she saw us go; for it was at Skanderborg Station, there she stood alone. But I went north, over land and sea, and summer-drunk knew me, and when I fell asleep on Himmelbjærget, those brown eyes burned me. They burned so sweetly, they burned so hotly. I dreamed I took her with me. She smelled of flowers, violets and reseda, and kissed me with relief and peace. Such strong kisses from an honorable mouth. Had the coffee not been served, the young Miss from Skanderborg must have compromised herself. Oh, these honorable citizens, they must have their hearts ached, the strong reseda blooms beautifully in the father's little garden. There are so many citizens, who make our thoughts fly away. (I can probably remember twenty with sky-blue and ten with brown eyes). There are so many delicate little ones, who gave us a dance and a rose, travel memories and elf-deceptions, that fade away by day over the bog! But these flowers from young years, I gathered them in heaps; and when I smell the fleeting scent, my blood begins to sing. They languish so sweetly, so heartbroken for sunshine and airy blue days. But it is at Skanderborg Station, where they all stand.

O Jesus Christ! Our Savior you are, Our hope you alone! Beyond all deceit So fervently We believe in you, Your pure word comforts us! As you yourself will, Our cause you order, You Israel's light in darkness! You are such a proud Master! Teach us your commandments, And let, as our God, Us worship you, Lord Jesus! We belong to you, And be we will, Wherever you yourself would have us most; With blind love, We let you in, In heart and mind, With grace, your gift of strength! So fervently We believe in you, our King! And so trust in your grace, Like a friend in need; For us, sweet Lord! Your death was full-hearted, You save from all kinds of trouble! Yes, now and always, Our firm trust We have with us: In danger and sorrow Your word is our comfort, Your living voice We hear with joy of heart! If sorrow comes upon us, Your heart's desire Is always our home; In danger and fear, Even if the darkness is thick, We follow you safely, Our soul in your hand command! Now we know for sure, Blessed Christ! You will never leave us! Yes, that is our covenant And you yourself have said, You have all power, So death cannot harm us! O, grant it God, We, according to your command, May be with you together, So that with you In heaven Eternal Can live in joy and old age!

An old grove stands in a wide field; in the afternoon the Vistula flows quietly. Its clear waters have been muddied with silt: and the ground in that grove is covered with rubble, and the harvest in the field is beaten to the straw; perhaps a wild storm raged there. Beneath the grove a desolate meadow spreads out, and on that meadow a soldier rests. A handsome soldier's face — two wilted lilies: a hundred-year-old linden tree bends over, and its yellow leaves fall palely on his face, and the soldier does not wake up, for he no longer lives. — A wild storm did not rage there, but an unfortunate war raged, so that the Lord God might erase it from human memory in the field above the Vistula, where the grove stands, there two of their kind fought to the death; a Russian and a Polish, brothers, children of one mother. — That is our curse! — Our eternal quarrels have laid our Glory-mother — on a bier, and Slavic freedom has fallen into the yoke, but God willing, that holy hour will strike, when the ancient curse will be lifted from us and brother will give his hand to brother for eternal peace. — The brothers fought one day — and the second: on the third at dawn the fierce battle roared, around the grove above the Vistula, in a distant space, Rus like a sea spilled over those plains; Lach struck it — not even a wild gale: the gale raged — and the sea remained only a sea. — Then our soldier stood in silence, in pain, there on that sad field of fratricide, where the Slavian man waded in Slavic blood; saw brother carrying brother to destruction, and he suddenly grabbed his sword, broke it — and threw it far into the field. And the field was covered with black clouds, and from that cloud the cannons thundered, and a terrible flood of bullets rolled down on the regiments: and all around on the wide plain the brave Slavs perish regiment after regiment, and the clear waters of the Vistula muddy the blood of Slavs. And my soldier turned pale to a lily, and towards his brothers, where brothers fight, he looked back once more and groaned in grief: 'To you, my God, my blood is offered as a sacrifice, only sanctify the brothers, sanctify them for peace!' Všeslav cried out wounded, fell and died.

You, my soul, the soul of youth, fly across the vastness of the world, fly across the world of the sons of Slavism, like a virgin dove flying over a grove and flying, looking for a green branch, on which to rest, when the storm blows, your longing soul. — You, my soul, fly widely, and where freedom welcomes you, where the sun of glory is yet to rise, rest your longing eye: there you will rest, there you will immerse yourself into the depths of beautiful nature, from love, from beauty, from faith you will create your own world of holy freedom. I dream of lands where there is no sin, where desire is already a pleasure, where a great consciousness looms — like the Kremlin's golden roof over holy Moscow — over the spring heart, where youth is eternally green, where against murderers flying out to the old holy anger means freedom, where you don't hear the cries of need, except for the sweet needs of the soul, where there is no night, where the day smells like in that Mahmud sky: — I dream of these lands, but do you know such lands anywhere? — Only my soul itself bears witness to me — the rest of the world murmurs: nowhere! Oh, Mountain, Mountain! you Montenegro! You land of strong rule! Just look at those castles of yours: Balkans above, the depths of the sea! Such is your son as the Balkans, so strong, terrible, so proud, so free, such a great lord, so hard in his will! — And as the grey waters of the Adriatic, so deep is his feeling; as the storm of those waters, so wild is the son of your nature in revenge; as the eternal sea honors its laws, so your son the laws of his fathers: the roar of the sea, these are the bells of freedom in the breasts of your Montenegrins! — You, my soul, when feelings seize you through the vastness of the world, you fly alone with your only idea of ​​young life: in the families of Glory you fly widely, and there, where freedom welcomes you, where the sun of glory is still rising, you rest your longing eye: there you will rest, there you will immerse yourself in the beautiful mystery of nature, from love, beauty, from faith you will create your own world of holy freedom: now take off with your enthusiasm to the highest mountain of the Carpathians, to shine over the sleepy race with my reflection of that of our brothers!

Over the Tatra the sky is cloudy, clouded with thunderclouds; the murky Váh and Hron rivers roll through the regions withered by grief. The Váh and Hron rivers dew Slovakia, the Slovaks shed tears into it; Mother Tatra bears sorrow, rings ring to her children's graves. That grave for us, treachery has dug into that earth, for which the Slovak blood, has often been shed as a sacrifice. Do not grieve, Tatra, dear mother! Take off your dark robe; rejoice, — God will turn the treachery of the traitors back on their vile heads. And our region will be refreshed again and blossom with new flowers: The bright Váh and Hron rivers will run through the solid Slovak field.

The woodcarver, for having often rested on a block, He began to make a statue of Hercules from it. He hadn't even finished his hands, but the audacious knight Dissatisfied with being in the hall, he wanted to occupy the entire house. The woodcarver was frightened by such a grateful fruit; He cut off the arms and legs—the block remained a block.

There's no true friendship in the world now; The last example I know of it was in the Oszmiana district. There lived Mieszek, Leszek's friend, and Mieszek's friend. One of those who say: where you are, there I am, - what's mine is yours. They used to say about them that when they found a nut, they would split the seed in two; In short, such friends, The likes of which were few even then. You would say: two spirits in one body. About this friendship of theirs once in the shade of an oak grove, While they were chatting, blending their tender words, To the rooks' caws and the crows' croaks, At once something roared near them. Leszek to the oak tree; why not jump up and down the trunk like a woodpecker? Mieszek doesn't know this art, He just reaches out his hands from below: 'Kumie!' The comrade has already climbed to the top. Mieszko barely had time to narrow his eyes, To turn pale, to fall on his face: and already the bear is stalking. He stumbles upon the body, feels it: it looks like a corpse; He smells it: and from that smell, Which could have been the result of fear. He concludes that it's dead and that it's already stale. So, with a mutter of contempt, he turns back to the forest, Because a Lithuanian bear doesn't eat stale meat. Just then, Mieszko revived... 'You were a tough one!' The comrade calls out, 'Lucky you didn't get scratched!' But why was he panting over you for so long? As if he were whispering something in your ear?' 'He told me,' Mieszko said, 'a bear proverb: That we know true friends in times of need.'
